title: Michael Ovitz Ordered to Complete Deposition in Julia Ormond Case After Storming Out Over Jeffrey Epstein Questions
description: A judge on Thursday ordered CAA co-founder Michael Ovitz to complete his deposition in the Julia Ormond sexual assault lawsuit, months after stormin
body:
A judge on Thursday ordered CAA co-founder Michael Ovitz to complete his deposition in the Julia Ormond sexual assault lawsuit, months after storming out when he was asked about Jeffrey Epstein.

	Ormond is suing CAA for arranging a meeting for her with Harvey Weinstein in December 1995, after which Weinstein allegedly sexually assaulted her. Ovitz had already left the agency at that point, but Ormond’s lawyers have sought to question him about the agency’s relationship with Weinstein and about how it handled sexual misconduct issues.
	

	At a deposition on June 1, Ovitz grew irate when Ormond’s lawyers asked him if he was friendly with Epstein, the notorious sex criminal. 


	“What does this got to do with Harvey Weinstein?” Ovitz asked, before taking off his microphone and storming out.

	Ormond’s lawyers asked the judge in the case to issue an arrest warrant and to hold Ovitz in contempt. Ovitz, meanwhile, asked to be excused from further questioning on the grounds that Ormond’s lawyers were trying to harass him with irrelevant questions.

	In his ruling on Thursday, Judge Adam Silvera ordered Ovitz to complete his deposition by Dec. 18. He denied the requests for an arrest warrant and a contempt finding, but also refused to rule out further questions about Epstein.

	“The Court finds that the deposition of non-party Ovitz was not completed but, rather was inappropriately terminated by non-party Ovitz,” the judge ruled.

	Ormond’s lawyers issued a statement on Thursday applauding the ruling.

	“We are pleased that the Court has held that Michael Ovitz ‘inappropriately terminated’ the deposition, required him to return and answer all of our questions, and ‘warned’ him to follow the Court’s rules,” said the attorneys, Kevin Mintzer, Meredith Firetog, and Effie Blassberger. “The decision makes clear that Mr. Ovitz was not entitled to storm out of the deposition, and that he is not above the law. We look forward to resuming the deposition and trust that Mr. Ovitz will behave himself.”
	

	Emails between Ovitz and Epstein were disclosed earlier this year as part of the Epstein files. In one email, Ovitz states that he was looking forward to seeing Epstein at St. Barts, and in another he writes, “I would love to see you.”

	CAA’s lawyers argued that Ovitz had been ambushed with material designed to smear his character rather than reveal anything relevant to the case.

title: Indian Premier League Stands Alone at the Top as Asia Pacific Sports Rights Growth Slows, Media Partners Asia Finds
description: The Indian Premier League remains the only Asia Pacific sports property priced at the top of the global market, according to new research from Media
body:
The Indian Premier League remains the only Asia Pacific sports property priced at the top of the global market, according to new research from Media Partners Asia, which expects growth in the region’s sports rights fees to slow to 1%–2% a year through 2030, down from about 10% a year since 2021.

	The cricket league earns about $12.4 million a match, in line with the Premier League, MPA said. Korea’s KBO baseball league earns about $100,000. India accounted for more than half of the increase in the region’s rights fees since 2021, and 64% of all fees is now concentrated in the 12 most valuable rights packages.
	

	The figures come from “APAC’s Sports Economy and Where Value Goes Next,” an MPA report covering 14 markets that draws on the company’s tracking of 150-plus rights contracts across properties and markets. MPA has published a summary of that report alongside findings from “APAC Sports Fandom: The Consumer’s Voice,” a companion study by ampd, MPA’s data and analytics arm, which polled 10,249 fans across six markets. The summary coincides with the second edition of MPA’s APOS Sports Edge forum, held at The METT in Singapore in the run-up to the city’s Formula 1 Grand Prix weekend.


	MPA puts the region’s commercial sports economy at $16.2 billion in 2026. Media rights are the biggest category, worth $6.1 billion, followed by sponsorship at $4.7 billion, ticketing and hospitality at $3.9 billion and merchandise at $1.5 billion.

	Rights fees rose 58% over five years to $5.7 billion. The wider sports economy is projected to expand by around 5% annually, reaching roughly $19.5 billion by 2030, with sponsorship and ticket sales doing most of the lifting.
	

	Streaming services paid 50% of rights fees this year, up from 36% in 2021. MPA said streamers now determine pricing in most markets. Yet just 3% of lapsed fans who returned to a sport did so because it appeared on a platform they already used, according to MPA.

	“This is not the end of sport’s boom in Asia Pacific. It is the end of the easy part,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of MPA.

	Couto said the region generates about $4 in commercial sports revenue per person, compared with upward of $200 in North America. “That gap is not a ceiling. It is headroom. The next dollar will come from the seat, the sponsor, the local star and the women’s game, and it will go to the rights-holders who know their fans by name,” he said.

	MPA estimates that sponsorship priced on audience data could grow 6%–7% a year to 2030. In China, India, Korea and Southeast Asia, sponsorship spending as a share of GDP trails the worldwide benchmark. If those markets made up half of that shortfall, the region would gain about $5.4 billion a year, the company said.

	The report singles out Japan, women’s competitions and homegrown stars as the areas most likely to draw competing bids. Japan’s subscription streaming market, worth $6.4 billion, is six times the size of its sports rights fees. In India, the final of the 2025 Women’s Cricket World Cup drew 185 million digital viewers, and MPA expects contested bidding for women’s properties, beginning with the WPL’s 2028 rights cycle.

	Home-grown properties are already pulling crowds. KBO attendance reached 12.3 million in 2025, a record, up from 7.3 million in 2019, while more than 25 million viewers in Japan watched the opening game of Major League Baseball’s 2025 Tokyo Series. The Nippon-Ham Fighters posted revenue 59% above 2019 levels in their first year as owners of Es Con Field.

	MPA tallied roughly $14 billion of investment and ownership changes in APAC sport since 2021, the bulk of it in IPL franchises and venues. The company argued that the spending has so far secured scarce assets without generating cash flow.

	The ampd fan research, conducted online in Indonesia, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Thailand and Australia and supplemented by 1,029 video interviews, found that personal connections are the most common route into a sport for new fans. Some 35% of respondents who picked up a sport for the first time were introduced by someone they knew, against 14% who came in through a major event. And 63% of fans who spent money on sport over the past year bought no subscription.
	

	Creators also hold fans’ attention. Independent creators capture 42%–43% of sports viewing hours on YouTube in Korea and Thailand, while league and club channels take 10%–19%. And 84% of fans who track players, pundits or creators spent on sport last year, compared with 43% of those who track none.

	“Fans follow their country, their club and the player from home, and global leagues win fans here through a local star,” said Dhivya T, head of insights at ampd and MPA, who is presenting the fan research at the forum.

	More than 30 speakers are taking part in the full-day event, including Liberty Media president and CEO Derek Chang, LaLiga president Javier Tebas, JioStar vice chair Uday Shankar, Prime Video Sport International managing director Alex Green, Tving CEO Julie Choi and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team CEO Peter Bayer, along with executives from the Bundesliga, the J.League, Netflix and YouTube.

title: ‘Angel and the Badman’ Review: Zachary Levi Leads Angel Studios’ Fitfully Engaging Remake of a John Wayne Vehicle
description: Inevitably the Angel media company and streaming platform, rebranded from Angel Studios in 2025, has remade the 1947 John Wayne project “Angel and t
body:
Inevitably the Angel media company and streaming platform, rebranded from Angel Studios in 2025, has remade the 1947 John Wayne project “Angel and the Badman,” and not just for the angelic title. It’s actually the third iteration; a 2009 Hallmark Channel adaptation, shot in wintry British Columbia instead of the dusty, sandy American West, starred Lou Diamond Phillips and Deborah Kara Unger. The latest, directed by Julio Quintana, stars Zachary Levi and is fitfully diverting, draped with calming New Mexico scenery.
	

	The first version, Wayne’s self-financed debut as producer as well as star, came from Republic Pictures and veteran screenwriter James Edward Grant, who went on to write another 11 Wayne films. The gamble was in Wayne’s decision to hire Grant as a first-time director. Intriguingly balanced sagebrush-and-six-gun romcom one minute, leisurely drama of redemption the next, “Angel and the Badman” presented Wayne as Quirt Evans, a gunman and cattle rustler saved from his violent past and and varmint future by a chance encounter with a Quaker frontier family. The Worth clan, especially the demure yet hungry-eyed adult daughter Penny, played by Gail Russell, nurses Quirt back to health after his opening-credits shootout with the Laredo gang — of which Quirt’s a member, looking to get out.


	 Of the three, the first movie remains the most compelling. It wasn’t the first Quaker oater — “The Lady from Cheyenne” preceded it, and “High Noon” and “Cheyenne Autumn” followed, along with the not-actual-Western “Friendly Persuasion” — but it’s most character-specific and flavorful of the versions. The new film, with its blend of Christian virtues and righteous bloodshed, may well connect with audiences hip to distributor Angel’s business model guided by “values-based” stories (per the website language) that “amplify light and bring more goodness into the world,” and “reintroduce positive values to the entertainment industry.”
	

	What works here? Tommy Lee Jones certainly does, in the old Harry Carey role of the wily, philosophical U.S. Marshall who has his eye on Quirt and the Laredo gang. He’s 80 years old, and thankfully Jones hasn’t done anything to look otherwise. But his voice is higher now, and his delivery of even the cardboard-iest of lines offers witty little payoffs. The downside of Jones being the upside of his own movie is simple: There are times when you’d rather be watching a whole movie about this guy.

	As Quirt, Zachary Levi is, well, a number of different things. A lot of his role, as written, leans into anachronistic wisenheimer mode, with rejoinders like “goodbyes ain’t never really been my thing” or, when rescuing the woman he loves from a fate worse than death, a quippy “Sorry I’m late!” Elsewhere in the film, Quirt must reckon with the legacy of brutality left to him by his father, and by his own livelihood in recent years. Levi can’t reconcile the tonal swings, but he’s proficient, if more in the vein of Jason Sudekis/Ted Lasso than in the creation of dimensional dark angel. (That title always referred to two angels, not one.)

	The Quaker religion has been replaced here by all-purpose Christian belief and believers represented, variously, by the townsfolk — it’s a very small town with very few extras — and this remake’s depiction of the Worth family. Meg Fraser’s scrappy, yearning Penny works well enough, though visually and in terms of character, “Angel and the Badman” smoothes much of the western texture and atmosphere. Allowing for the notion of brand new towns uneasily sprouting alongside the railroad tracks, the film shows us little of life, and stuff, as it might have looked in the 19th-century west. Every belt buckle looks freshly yanked off the rack; every speck of signage resembles something painted 45 minutes before filming commenced that day.

	Cinematographer and editor Alex Quintana’s lighting, cutting and shot design — to the degree he worked with the director on the third element — gets the job done without fuss but also without distinction, or surprises. Frustratingly, the first shot of the film is the strongest: a well-judged long-distance view of a lone rider on the horizon, after we’ve heard gunshots from off-screen, soon joined by horsemen in pursuit. We’ve seen a few like it before, but this one’s framed judiciously, and doesn’t look or feel like just another reenactment of a cliche.
	

	The frustration arrives all too soon. There’s very little piety in the 1947 film, and there’s serious chemistry between Wayne and Russell. The new “Angel and the Badman” trades those virtues for plenty of sanctimony and not much of a spark.

schema.headline: ‘Angel and the Badman’ Review: Zachary Levi Leads Angel Studios’ Fitfully Engaging Remake of a John Wayne Vehicle

title: Hugh Hefner’s Widow Crystal Harris Asks Jessica Biel to ‘Please Reconsider’ Playing His Wife: ‘I Experienced Sexual, Emotional…Physical Abuse’
description: Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional ver
body:
Crystal Harris, who was married to Playboy founder Hugh Hefner until his death in 2017, is asking Jessica Biel to reconsider playing a fictional version of Hefner’s wife in the upcoming film “Playmates.”

	After Biel’s casting was announced, Harris posted her message to Biel on Instagram, saying “Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner’s wife if this film intends to romanticize him or the Playboy world. I was actually his wife, and I experienced sexual, emotional, financial and physical abuse in that relationship.”
	

	Lorraine Nicholson, the daughter of Jack Nicholson, is writing and directing the Searchlight film that also stars Bill Pullman as Hefner as well as Lily-Rose Depp and “The HousemaidIndiana Elle. 


	“Many other woman have come forward with allegations of rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation as well,” Harris wrote, “There are also deeply troubling concerns involving minors. I hope everyone involved this film takes the time to listen the women who lived it before helping Hollywood turn it back into nostalgia.” 

	After Hefner’s death, Harris revealed her experiences at the “toxic” Playboy mansion in her 2024 memoir “Only Say Good Things: Surviving Playboy and Finding Myself.”

	According to the synopsis, the “Playmates” movie revolves around “Elle (Elle), a 13-year-old know-it-all who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home, and meets Anna (Depp), one of seven hopefuls vying to be Playmate of the Month. The two form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what the other wants most, a magazine cover and a boy.” Nicholson has written for magazines about her childhood experiences at the Playboy Mansion.

title: ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Season 28 Premiere Recap: A Gang Rape Echoing the Cornell 7 Case
description: “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” is renowned for its ripped-from-the-headlines episodes. Who can forget the Trayvon Martin-Paula Deen crossover f
body:
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” is renowned for its ripped-from-the-headlines episodes. Who can forget the Trayvon Martin-Paula Deen crossover featuring Cybill Shepherd as a racist celebrity chef or the Gamergate-riffing “Intimidation Game,” where Ice-T shoots Logan Paul’s misogynistic geek on a Manhattan rooftop?

	The Season 28 premiere of “SVU,” on Oct. 8 on NBC, wasn’t a play on the news by design. According to showrunner Michele Fazekas, the episode was written and shot in July.  But it will feel incredibly timely given its similarities to the Cornell 7 gang rape case — which “SVU” star Mariska Hargitay has publicly condemned, calling for justice to be served.
	

	Titled “Volition,” the episode concerns Emily (Lizzy DeClement), a young woman who’s discovered in a subway car dizzy and disheveled. She believes she was gang-raped by a group of three men — two of whom she knew, including a man named Josh — while she was passed out from consuming too much alcohol. At the hospital, she claims she “doesn’t remember” and initially blames herself, prompting Benson (Hargitay) to assure Emily, “Was it the best idea to drink that much? It wasn’t. Does that mean that anyone is allowed to touch you or do anything to you without your consent?” “I guess not,” Emily replies, adding, “Look: The nurse said to just say that I passed out. I could say that if it helps my case.” But Benson advises her to stick to the truth.


	Back at the station, the male detectives of “SVU” seem to disagree over whether someone with Emily’s .17 blood alcohol content can give consent. “You can’t give consent when you’re that drunk,” offers Det. Griffin (Corey Cott). “Legally, drunk people can give consent… Think about any girl you had sex with in college — were they drunk? Did you get consent?” fires back Det. Bruno (Kevin Kane). Benson cuts through the noise, declaring, “The law says that a victim has to be physically helpless or given an intoxicating substance without consent,” leading Griffin to reply, “Then the law is garbage.” Benson concurs: “I couldn’t agree with you more. And legislature even tried to change it this summer, but the session ran out before there was a vote, so we’re stuck with this garbage.” (As Fazekas told Variety, this law is real, and she thinks “it’s part of why law enforcement declines to prosecute” cases like the alleged Cornell gang rape when the victim was drunk — “and I hope that’s something that is talked about more,” she added.)
	



	Det. Griffin and Capt. Curry (Aimé Donna Kelly) question the three men. One of the suspects, Scott, works for a tech startup and claims the night was “weird” but consensual, and involved Josh, Daniel (his cousin), Emily and himself at Josh’s mom’s place. “Eventually we were in the bedroom, and I can safely say I’ve never done anything like that… Have sex with someone and then watch other people have sex with that person,” he says. When Det. Griffin presses him on whether she offered consent, he says, “She didn’t say ‘no’ and she was acting very into it.” Sgt. Tutuola (Ice-T) questions Daniel, a guy with a girlfriend sticking to the same story, and Sgt. Rollins (Kelli Giddish) and Det. Bruno take on Josh, a lab technician friendzoned by Emily, who hints at culpability by refusing to engage with the police and may be “the weak link.” Meanwhile, Josh’s mom won’t cooperate with Benson, though she thinks she can crack her.

	And indeed, she does. The mother shows Benson incriminating footage captured by the home cameras of Scott and Daniel goading Josh into not “missing an opportunity” with Emily since she’s so “wasted” that he can “do whatever you want to her, she’s not going to remember in the morning.” The three men then cheer, and go back into the apartment.

	The case goes to court, where ADA Carisi (Peter Scavino) is joined by ADA Aidan Hawkins (Jelani Alladin), a recent graduate of Harvard Law, in taking up Emily’s cause. There’s also Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron), a veteran jury consultant who helps them bounce a couple of questionable jurors. “I’d be worried about any woman who you put on this jury,” she tells Benson. “They project themselves onto the victim: ‘I would never put myself in that position, this could never happen to me,’ therefore the victim is to blame.” She adds, rather ominously, “I don’t think this will go the way you want it to… You have faith in the system [and] I hope you’re right. I just wouldn’t have gone to trial with this.”

	At trial, defense attorney Andrea Vargas (Lindsay Mendez) grills Emily on the stand: “You can’t honestly sit here right now and say whether or not you consented?” “Did you push them away and make them stop… or were you encouraging them?” “You never said ‘no,’ did you Emily? And then when you woke up, you changed your mind!” The callousness of her questioning brings Emily to tears.
	

	Vargas subsequently offers Carisi a deal: The men will cop to misdemeanor “forcible touching” — it won’t get them any extra time in jail, but will land them on the sex offender registry. Carisi urges Benson to accept the deal otherwise “they’re gonna walk,” and Hawkins sides with Benson in fighting it out, sparking conflict between the ADA and the commanding officer. A hung jury makes the case go to a retrial.



	

					Olivia Benson (Mariska Hargitay) and Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron) strategize in “Law & Order: SVU.”
									Virginia Sherwood/NBC
	



	Following the ruling, Benson drowns her sorrows over cocktails with Sharpe, and, in a revealing, impeccably acted scene, airs out her grievances about her job. “We don’t stop anything. We don’t prevent a crime from happening. We just pick up the pieces afterwards,” she says. “Nothing has changed. We’re 30 years in, and a jury gets to decide that if a woman drinks too much, then she deserves to be raped. That is the problem.” Sharpe’s advice to Benson is to “fight differently,” so she does, arresting Josh’s mother on trumped-up charges of evidence tampering and conspiracy to commit rape (with Hawkins’ approval, who signs off on the warrant) to flip Josh. The sketchy gambit works, and Josh agrees to testify against his pals in exchange for a lesser charge and the release of his mom, but inflames tensions between Benson and Carisi, infuriated that she’d gone behind his back.

	Josh testifies during the retrial that as she lay in bed with Emily that night, she kept requesting her phone to order an Uber home, but the men had hidden it from her. Then, Scott and Daniel entered the room as Emily was passed out and all three men took turns raping her as she went in and out of consciousness. “She had no idea what was going on for most of it,” he confessed. “I’ve been thinking about her so much and fantasizing, and I convinced myself that she wanted it. That if she was awake, she would have wanted it.”

	Scott and Daniel are found guilty of rape in the first degree — as Benson exits the courtroom, however, she locks eyes with Carisi and a look of guilt washes over her face. She got the result she wanted, but at what cost?

	According to Hargitay, “Volition” held special importance for her due to the current laws surrounding consent, stating that if survivors choose to consume drinks or drugs they “cannot legally claim that they were unable to consent to sex — unless they were physically unconscious or unable to speak.”
	

	She continued: “This is a voluntary intoxication loophole. It exists in 19 states. Legislators had the opportunity to address it and failed. Now is the time to let them know: These outdated laws must change.”

title: Ice-T on ‘Law & Order: SVU’s’ Longevity and Cultural Impact: ‘I’m on a Good Treadmill, and I Want to Stay on It’
description:
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” has been running since 1999, and Ice-T has been there since almost the beginning.

	The rapper turned a four-epi
body:
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” has been running since 1999, and Ice-T has been there since almost the beginning.

	The rapper turned a four-episode stint in the show’s second season into a permanent role as Detective Odafin “Fin” Tutuola. Nearly 30 years later, as the show gears up for the premiere of its 28th season, Ice-T sat down to talk about his career and the cultural impact of “Law & Order: SVU” at the Variety Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage presented by OUTFRONT.
	

	Ice-T recalled being told he was the longest-running actor in U.S. television history after 21 seasons of “SVU.” He attributed the show’s staying power to the nature of the series: “First off, it’s a whodunit. Everybody loves a whodunit. Secondly, it’s not only entertainment; it’s also therapy.”

	His co-star Mariska Hargitay created the Joyful Heart Foundation in 2004 to support survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence and child abuse. Ice-T described the thank-yous he has received from women who saw justice served on the show that they might not have seen in real life, and said he was proud to be part of something that has been so impactful.

	Ice-T credits his musician background as helping him know how to interact with fans. Music is also where his passion still lies. “For me to be in films and television is fun, but doing music is a whole ‘nother thing because I write, produce and direct the whole thing.”

	He and Hargitay branched out into another realm with a Capital One commercial that aired during the Emmys — which Hargitay hosted. It was something Ice-T had done before, but his co-star had not. Still, he joked that she was “the star of the show” while filming the spot.
	

	The “SVU” crew also pretaped an Emmys sketch with Taylor Swift, which Ice-T likened to filming with then-Vice President Joe Biden during Season 18. “When you meet — I hate to say the word — the stars, you can tell they’re special,” he said. Swift’s cat, named after Hargitay’s Olivia Benson character, also made a cameo in the sketch. Ice-T joked that the cat must have been high on catnip, but both star and feline were “mad cool.”

	After so many years in the industry, Ice-T said what keeps him engaged is seeing his family happy. “All this other stuff, I’ve kind of been there, done that. Got the T-shirt,” he said. “I’ve achieved the accolades. I’ve done all this stuff.” He added, “I’m on a treadmill, but I’m on a good treadmill, and I want to stay on it.”

	The conversation with Ice-T was preceded by a panel discussing the power of culture and NBC’s 100th anniversary, moderated by Savannah Sellers, NBC News NOW anchor and NBC News correspondent. Joining Sellers were Mark Marshall, chairman of advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal; Rachael Zaluzec, chief marketing officer at Volkswagen and Julie Scelzo, chief creative officer at Xfinity.

	For Marshall, the compelling part of the brand equity that comes with an anniversary like NBC’s centennial is the generational aspect. “We have 22-year-olds who start every week at our company, and they all get in the elevator and take a picture of the peacock carpeting,” he said. Although people consume NBC’s content in different ways than in 1926, they still consume it.

	It’s a cultural moment like this that makes Zaluzec eager to get involved. Volkswagen created a commercial in partnership with “SNL’s” 50th anniversary last year in a spin on the classic “The Californians” sketch.

	At Xfinity, Scelzo sees these moments as an avenue to tap into culture in a relevant way: “When I really look beyond the idea of connecting you to stories of love throughout 100 years, we are literally the connection into your home to connect you to culture.”

	Zaluzec emphasized the importance of maintaining authenticity while capitalizing on cultural moments. Following up the “SNL” 50 ad, she said, was about creating something that served VW’s needs now.
	

	“You can’t force yourself into the moment, right?” Scelzo echoed. “You’re going to have to earn your right to be there.”

	Xfinity sponsored a countdown clock to NBCUniversal’s 100th anniversary special on Dec. 10. “It’s one thing to capitalize on the moment,” Szelco said of the activation. “It’s another way to show up in a way that feels meaningful.”

	Marshall emphasized the unique nature of a collective experience, particularly across generations. “Streaming had become kind of a siloed event,” he said. “Part of the reason live is having this rebirth is it’s a communal experience.”

schema.headline: Ice-T on ‘Law & Order: SVU’s’ Longevity and Cultural Impact: ‘I’m on a Good Treadmill, and I Want to Stay on It’

title: ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director’s Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller
description: It’s for the best that “Animals,” actor Ben Affleck‘s sixth outing behind the camera, is being released directly to Netflix — not that this slick, p
body:
It’s for the best that “Animals,” actor Ben Affleck‘s sixth outing behind the camera, is being released directly to Netflix — not that this slick, pacy serving of all-star pulp couldn’t or wouldn’t hold one’s attention in the multiplex. But ever since Affleck’s rousing, enjoyable political drama “Argo” won a Best Picture Oscar that it perhaps didn’t entirely need, his subsequent efforts have been burdened with the weighty expectations of a prestige filmmaker — the noirish, overbaked flop “Live by Night” certainly didn’t benefit from those, and while the fleet-footed crowdpleaser “Air” rallied nicely, it wasn’t a major work either. Affleck is, at heart, an audience-minded journeyman: Screwy and silly when it doesn’t sporadically hit you with a stray hard truth, “Animals” is disposable pulp, but it benefits from its director-star’s unassuming professionalism.  
	

	“He can’t enforce laws that he doesn’t abide,” says Abigail (Kerry Washington), the perfectly put-together wife of Affleck’s character Mark Kimball, a wealthy Los Angeles attorney now pivoting to politics with a well-funded mayoral run. The second she says it, mere minutes into proceedings, is when you know we’re about to wade through some extreme moral murk — heavily contrived by Affleck with co-writers Billy Ray and Connor O. McIntyre. At its most incisive, the film hits the pressure points of good, needling political satire, and if it pressed them just a little longer and harder, we could have had something quite potent here. But “Animals” also has other, more lurid matters to attend to — some heated marital melodrama, some hollow “what would you do” button-pushing — and if these high-low tonal extremes strip the film of some gravitas, they keep it plenty gripping.
	

	“Animals” opens with one of Mark’s extended campaign ads — a knowingly smarmy compilation of buzzwords and patently false man-of-the-people imagery, hitting all the necessary demographic targets, and working awfully hard to conceal the fact that the former lawyer and his family occupy an enviable Beverly Hills property worth over $10 million. So far, the people aren’t quite buying it: As Mark’s all-business campaign manager Sam (a disappointingly flat role for Steven Yeun) informs him, he’s still lagging in the polls, with the city’s Latin vote especially far from his grasp. How can that be, when he and Abigail are so good to their Mexican nanny Cecilia (“Emilia Pérez” standout Adriana Paz)? 

	Well, good within legal limits: When Cecilia asks if they could possibly offer some work to her boyfriend, illegal immigrant Ramon (Luis Gerardo Méndez), Abigail briskly explains that doing so could endanger her husband’s campaign. Still, it’s Halloween, and she and Mark trust Ramon enough to take their son Denny (Christopher Woodley) out trick-or-treating with his own, while they attend to more important matters: more campaign prep for Mark, and an online tryst with an extramarital lover for Abigail. So when Mark gets a call from a malevolent mystery predator, claiming that he’s taken Denny and demanding a $7 million ransom, multiple streams of guilt come into play.

	What begins as a fairly straightforward kidnapping thriller is ratcheted by turns into something more complicated, if not exactly complex, by a neat series of twists. A couple of those are easily forecast, but the crucial one is fiendishly spring-loaded, deftly shifting the stakes of the whole enterprise, and testing Mark’s integrity both as a man and as a politician. Affleck, always at his best in roles that place his all-American alpha qualities under a harsh, sweat-inducing spotlight, has cast himself ideally here. His performance, at first glib, is so convincingly unnerved that you almost don’t need the faintly absurd foil character of Dayle Burton (Gillian Anderson) to tighten the screws. 

	An enigmatic British fixer called on by Sam to secure the ransom — since Mark’s fortune has largely been sunk into his campaign — Dayle’s purpose is mainly to strut around the place with intimidating serenity in a crisp white pantsuit, and to deliver dialogue like “Everyone’s beholden to something, that’s big boy life” in a cut-glass accent that only renders it more ludicrous. Her arrival is most entertaining, and also a clear signal of the film’s imminent takeover by its own trashiest instincts: Little in “Animals” rings true from here on out, but you still want to know where it’s heading, and how snakily it’s going to get there.
	

	Still, for a few tantalizing minutes after its biggest bombshell, the film dangles the possibility of something starkly and breathtakingly true: a glimpse of America at its cruellest and most unequal. It never matches that — despite a broadly satirical and rather amusing coda that deservedly pokes fun at a national tradition of macho personality politics. The rest of the filmmaking, too, is content to coast at a lower difficulty setting, from the proficient but anonymously taupe lensing by master DP Robert Elswit to an untested ensemble of ever-watchable actors playing capably to type. “Animals” is a tart, nasty diversion, where it could be something uglier and more lingering. But you can’t blame Affleck for instead just getting the job coolly and efficiently done.

schema.headline: ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director’s Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller

title: ‘Other Mommy’ Review: Jessica Chastain’s Doppelgänger Horror Misfires in Every Direction
description: If you enjoyed watching the trailer for “Other Mommy” during every multiplex outing this summer, you’ll get an extended dose of its freneticism duri
body:
If you enjoyed watching the trailer for “Other Mommy” during every multiplex outing this summer, you’ll get an extended dose of its freneticism during the actual film — right down to an opening title card that appears letter-by-letter while intercut with choppy action. From director Rob Savage, and adapted from the horror novel “Incidents Around the House,” the finished product is among the most limp and ineffectual works to grace the screen this year, misfiring in every direction, including and especially its tone.
	

	It plays, at times, as though a horror comedy in the vein of Sam Raimi had been recut at the 11th hour to resemble a straightforward scarefest, down to missing chunks one imagines had been ripped out by hand. The saga begins with what feels like a second act and continues in a constant state of climax, with an endless litany of numbing jump scares that grow quickly stale, since they all unfold pretty much the same way. More often than not, the camera tracks around an unsuspecting character in a circle, revealing from behind them the eponymous Other Mommy (Jessica Chastain, delivering a grin that’s more goofy than unsettling), a demonic being posing little actual threat. The effort at trying to make this work a hundred different ways would be adorable if it weren’t so grating.


	When the story opens, adolescent protagonist Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) is already familiar with the creature hiding in her bedroom, who takes the form of her mother Ursula (Chastain). It isn’t long before her father Russell (Jay Duplass) catches a glimpse of the monster too, when it taunts them in the kitchen one morning, leading to a straight-faced premise where everyone readily accepts that there’s a sinister copy of Ursula hiding somewhere in their home, and contorting her body in the shape of a swastika for no real reason. When most other horror movies feature skeptical naysayers, they do so for the sake of building tension and intrigue; “Other Mommy” doesn’t seem interested in these things.
	

	Despite gazing at the ghostly presence in full, Bela’s parents don’t seem all that spooked, even when the young girl is tossed around like a rag doll during an anniversary gathering at their home. No human character seems to behave like a real person, and the Other Mommy is merely an impish rogue along the lines of Pennywise the Clown, minus the child eating. It’s a movie of psychological pranks involving ball pits, wonky gravity, and a CGI Chastain alternatingly melting like the Batman villain Clayface and flailing about like an inflatable tube man outside a secondhand car dealership. All the while, there’s seldom a sense of scale or proximity to put any of this into physical perspective.

	There are the bare bones of a story and theme if you squint, in that Bela suspects her mother of having an affair. So, the idea that Ursula is not who she appears to be makes for a worthwhile entry point into a tale of an eerie, dead-eyed copy — at least in theory. In practice, this mischievous presence ping-pongs between maternal lies and the wholesale impersonation of other people. This may be in keeping with the novel, but little of the movie’s condensed, 94-minute runtime feels guided by any visual or emotional idea; it all but abandons the “Mommy” half of its premise before long.

	In addition, each of the three leads seems to belong to a markedly different movie. Chastain goes for broke with melodrama as both the real and fake Mommies. Clark, although she plays younger and more naive than her actual age, maintains a captivating, naturalistic presence, until she seems to get exhausted by the premise (who can blame her?) And Duplass, with his “aw, shucks” demeanor, reads like a broad caricature out of a comedy sketch. It’s all over the place, and it isn’t made much better by the fact that scenes appear to begin and end at random without much flow or rhythm — a seeming result of “Other Mommy” being cut within an inch of its life.

	In the most basic sense, a film in which supernatural scares arise courtesy of negative space ought to at least have thoughtful framing, but the endless series of startles arrive with the same weight and energy as the fake outs. Tension dissipates no matter who or what jumps out from darkened spaces, as the movie veers between physical dangers and imaginary sequences as Chastain’s spiritual entity occupies young Bela’s attention like an annoying, persistent daydream. That’s about all that “Other Mommy” is to its audience too: an annoyance to be handwaved, rather than tension or meaning to be confronted at any stage. Feel free to keep your arms and legs outside the ride; it’s not going anywhere.

title: Fan Bingbing Says Young Chinese Audiences ‘Aren’t Being Fed Very Well’ as AI Microdramas Boom
description:
Fan Bingbing watches AI-generated microdramas now and then. She’s just not convinced they’re doing China’s young audiences any good.

	The Chinese s
body:
Fan Bingbing watches AI-generated microdramas now and then. She’s just not convinced they’re doing China’s young audiences any good.

	The Chinese star made the remarks at a Busan International Film Festival press conference, where she presented Wayne Wang’s “Diary of a Mad Old Man,” screening in the A Window on Asian Cinema strand, and Ivan Tan’s short “She Said,” which world premiered in the Wide Angle section’s Asian Short Film Competition. It’s her third visit to the festival.
	

	Pointing to the popularity of AI-generated microdramas in China, Fan questioned whether they offered younger viewers the artistic nourishment she had found in cinema. “I feel that young people in China aren’t being fed very well,” she said, referring to the screen content they consume.


	Fan pointed to Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” “Human performances contain so many emotions and expressions,” she said. “The performances in ‘Possible Love’ cannot be conveyed or replicated by AI.”

	At a special talk following the screening of Park Chan-wook’s “The Handmaiden,” her selection for the festival’s Carte Blanche program, Fan spoke of her fascination with the danger and freedom embodied by the film’s two female leads. “I first watched this film 10 years ago. Because it had never been released in China, I had to make a special effort to find a way to see it,” she said. “But the impact it had on me is just as powerful 10 years later.”

	She also recalled serving alongside Park on the Cannes jury in 2017, describing him as courteous and gentlemanly. Though he spoke sparingly, she said, “His observations were incisive.” Fan added that she would be delighted to work with him if the opportunity arose.
	

	Reflecting during the talk on what has sustained her commitment to acting over three decades, Fan placed her career within the wider development of Asian cinema, which she said had found its place and voice over the past two decades.

	“Actors of my generation in China hold themselves to an internal standard,” she said. “We belong to a generation that connects what came before with what comes next. We have a responsibility to carry that legacy forward, and we hope to be remembered ourselves.”

	Fan described her belief in “yuanfen,” the Chinese concept of affinity or connection shaped by fate. “You can’t force the connection between an actor and a role, or between an actor and a director,” she said. “But I believe that only by continually accumulating experience can you keep challenging who you are and extend your life as an actor.”

	Fan largely disappeared from Chinese screens after a 2018 tax evasion case. She has since worked outside China, winning the Golden Horse best leading actress award for Malaysian drama “Mother Bhumi” and starring in Korean-language feature “Green Night.”

	Fan joked that she had been “forced” to adapt as her work took her beyond a fixed screen image and across languages, though she said she was grateful for the pressures that had led her toward unexpected roles.

	“Following the storyline that fate gives me, and doing justice to my abilities as an actor, is already a source of happiness,” she said.

title: Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Surprise Premieres at NYCC and Earns Glowing First Reactions: ‘A Worthy Successor’ to ‘WandaVision’
description:
Marvel debuted the first episode of “VisionQuest” with a surprise screening to close out its New York Comic Con panel Thursday.

	Early reactions to
body:
Marvel debuted the first episode of “VisionQuest” with a surprise screening to close out its New York Comic Con panel Thursday.

	Early reactions to the Disney+ show, which is set to premiere Oct. 14, shared on social media were largely positive, and the perspectives ranged from con-goers who just saw the premiere episode to journalists who offered up their first brief reviews of the season when Marvel’s embargo lifted simultaneously with the panel’s conclusion at 5:45 pm ET.
	

	“#VisionQuest is a worthy successor to WandaVision and it feels like a love letter to Wanda Maximoff at times,” Nexus Point News’ Demet Koc wrote on X. “It tackles the themes of love, grief, generational trauma, and identity. The relationship between Tommy and Vision will leave you wanting more from this family. James Spader is a delight and Emily Hampshire is a surprisingly entertaining addition. More to come…”


	The show features Paul Bettany’s first live-action MCU role since “WandaVision,” the inaugural Marvel TV show on Disney+ that starred him and Elizabeth Olson’s Wanda/Scarlet Witch. That show takes place after Thanos kills Vision in “Avengers: Infinity War” by ripping the Mind Stone from his forehead, which throws Wanda into a depression over the death of her lover. 

	In “WandaVision,” the former heroine takes over a New Jersey town and creates a fake, sitcom-inspired world where she and a magically-created, amnesiac Vision live happily ever after with their two kids, Tommy and Billy. Once Wanda’s ruse is uncovered, the real Vision (now sporting a white costume) is reanimated and has his full memory restored. He flies off, and Wanda later seemingly dies after going full villain in “Doctor Stranger in the Multiverse of Madness.”
	

	Now, Bettany’s Vision appears in both android and human form in “VisionQuest” alongside several of Marvel’s other famous AI robots. James Spader returns as Ultron, Emily Hampshire is E.D.I.T.H., Orla Brady is F.R.I.D.A.Y., James D’Arcy is J.A.R.V.I.S., T’nia Miller is Jocasta, Lauren Morais is Lisa Molinari and Ruaridh Mollica is the grown-up version of Tommy Maximoff.

	“The chemistry between Paul Bettany & James Spader is off the charts, & #VisionQuest is a worthy conclusion to the #WandaVision trilogy,” Agents of Fandom’s TJ Zwarych wrote. “It drags a bit in the middle, but it’s an Easter Egg filled mystery that starts & ends beautifully well. Emily Hampshire is a sneaky all-star!”

	Brandon Davis, who co-hosted Thursday’s “Up Next From Marvel Television and Marvel Animation” NYCC panel with Marvel TV and animation chief Brad Winderbaum, shared in an X post: “#VisionQuest is a fantastic sequel to WandaVision. It’s smart, weird, ambitious, and creative with a beating father/son heart. My favorite part; it seems to love being a part of the MCU and embracing as many corners as it can. As a longtime fan, it’s very rewarding. Loved it.”

	See below for the first social media reactions to “VisionQuest.”

            Angelina Jolie's realtor is shooting down reports that Madonna bought the actress' famous Los Angeles mansion.
      
    
            Ernie Carswell, who co-listed Angelina's historic Cecil B. DeMille estate, said during a recent episode of "Real Talk," that Madge is NOT the buyer of the $24.75 million property.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            As TMZ first reported ... Angelina's mansion sold September 24 after being listed for nearly $30 million. We did not report the buyer’s identity.
      

            Several outlets later claimed Madonna purchased the home ... with The Real Deal citing Robb Report.
      
    
            But Carswell says that's not true ... though the real estate agent isn't revealing the buyer.
      
    
            Madonna had been linked to the property before the sale. The New York Post reported in August that her representatives arranged a private virtual tour of the estate after she expressed interest in buying it.
      
    
            The 11,000-square-foot mansion, which once belonged to legendary filmmaker Cecil B. DeMille, includes six bedrooms, 10 bathrooms, a guesthouse, pool house, gym, tea house and sweeping views of the Hollywood Hills.
      
    
            Angelina purchased the 2.1-acre property for $24.5 million in 2017 ... and ultimately sold it for $24.75 million.

body:
Pete Hegseth
                          Public Can Watch Firing Squad Execute The Fort Hood Shooter ...
                          Feds Will Stream It Live!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                October 8, 2026
                
                            2:16 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 8, 2026
                                4:20 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Pete Hegseth wants the public to be able to see the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan ... and a War Department official tells us it will be livestreamed.
      
    
            The Secretary of War went on Real America's Voice on Thursday to address President Trump's decision to reinstate the firing squad for former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            There hasn't been a public execution in the United States in over 90 years, but Hegseth promises, "we'll make sure that people are able to watch it and that it's public."
      
    
            Hegseth didn't go into detail, but we're told it will be streamed live for the public.
      

            As we previously reported ... the president's decision comes just days after Tennessee's attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection went horribly wrong, as she survived two doses of pentobarbital before being rushed to the hospital.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The U.S. military hasn't put anyone to death since 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth ... and the last military firing-squad execution was even longer ago -- Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot to death in France in 1945 for desertion during World War II.
      
    
            Hegseth's determined to make history here.
